title: OpenFerro: a unified framework for mesoscale ferroic dynamics and enhanced sampling
abstract: Modeling ferroic materials requires connecting microscopic fluctuations to collective dynamics over mesoscales. We introduce OpenFerro, a unified lattice-field dynamics framework that combines flexible Hamiltonians, automatic differentiation, parallel execution, and enhanced sampling. The same framework can simulate ferroelectric domain motion, magnetic disordering, and coupled spin-lattice thermodynamics. On four graphics processors, a bulk BaTiO$_3$ benchmark with long-range dipolar interaction reaches $840^3$ unit cells, representing 3 billion atoms through the retained lattice variables. We simulate polarization textures in a PbTiO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ superlattice spanning $0.8~μ\mathrm{m}$ laterally and a BaTiO$_3$ nanoparticle 200~nm in diameter, retaining unit-cell resolution. We also demonstrate enhanced-sampling simulations that reconstruct the polarization free-energy surface of bulk BaTiO$_3$ without a prescribed polynomial form. With moderate computational resources, OpenFerro achieves atomistic-resolution simulations at mesoscopic scales traditionally studied with continuum models.
summary: This paper presents OpenFerro, a novel, unified computational framework designed to simulate ferroic materials by coupling structural, magnetic, and lattice dynamics. By integrating automatic differentiation and enhanced sampling, it bridges the gap between atomistic simulations and continuum models, enabling the study of complex phase transitions and domain dynamics at unprecedented scales.
main_problem: The core challenge is developing a computational framework to accurately model ferroic materials by connecting microscopic fluctuations to collective dynamics across mesoscopic length and time scales.
main_result: The OpenFerro framework successfully simulates complex ferroic phenomena, such as domain motion and polarization free-energy reconstruction, at atomistic resolution across mesoscopic scales.
method: The authors introduce OpenFerro, a unified lattice-field dynamics framework that combines flexible Hamiltonians, automatic differentiation, parallel execution, and enhanced sampling techniques.
model_or_system: The framework is applied to ferroic materials like $	ext{BaTiO}_3$ and $	ext{PbTiO}_3/	ext{SrTiO}_3$ superlattices, allowing the simulation of coupled dynamics between structural displacements ($\mathbf{u}$), magnetic moments ($\mathbf{m}$), and strain ($\mathbf{\eta}$).
key_observables: Polarization textures, domain patterns, polarization free-energy surface, local dipole, and strain.
important_parameters: Mesoscopic scales (e.g., $0.8 \mu	ext{m}$ lateral size), unit-cell resolution, and temperature/pressure regimes for phase transition mapping.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that interactions can be defined as independent, modular, and differentiable Python functions, and that the effective Hamiltonians are sufficient to capture the physics.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the software architecture pipeline from Hamiltonians to simulation protocols. Figure 2 shows temperature dependence for polarization and magnetization in various ferroic systems.
paper_structure: The paper details the unified framework (OpenFerro) combining multiple physical degrees of freedom ($\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{m}, \mathbf{\eta}$) and computational tools (AD, GPU parallelism). It then demonstrates its capability across various systems ($	ext{BaTiO}_3$, bcc Fe, $	ext{SrMnO}_3$) and techniques (NPT, enhanced sampling) to map out phase diagrams and free-energy landscapes.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter, the use of automatic differentiation and coupling multiple coupled, non-linear dynamical fields ($\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{m}, \mathbf{\eta}$) in a unified, scalable framework is highly relevant to modeling complex open quantum systems where multiple interacting subsystems must be tracked.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 | Software architecture of OpenFerro. Built- in interactions and custom energy functions (left) enter a common automatic-differentiation and just-in-time compila- tion pipeline to generate the force engine. The custom func- tions can couple local modes u, spins m, and strain η. Lat- tice fields are distributed across GPUs (right), while simula- tion protocols (bottom) select structural optimization, NVE, NVT, NPT, or enhanced sampling. Material-specific energy functions remain independent of the simulation core.

Fig. 3 | Throughput and single-node scaling of BaTiO3 NPT dynamics. (a) Largest timed systems found by the memory-constrained size search (blue, left axis) and throughput at those sizes (orange, right axis). One cell-step advances all retained fields of one unit cell by a complete integration step. (b) Peak allocator memory per GPU and (c) parallel efficiency for L = 120, 240, 360, 480, and 600. Both panels use a logarithmic system-size axis. Parallel efficiency is the single-GPU step time divided by the GPU count and parallel step time. Timings are medians of three 100-step measurements after compilation and warmup, excluding trajectory output.

Figure 3(a) shows the capacity and corresponding throughput. Capacity increases from 6483 = 272.1 million unit cells on one GPU to 8403 = 592.7 mil- lion on four, while throughput increases from 0.520 to 0.955 billion cell-steps per second. The largest system spans 331.6 nm along each axis and represents 3 bil- lion atoms through the retained lattice fields. A com- plete integration step takes 0.620 s. At the smaller size of 4803 = 110.6 million cells (not shown in panel (a)), four GPUs reach 1.00 billion cell-steps per second.
